assumptions: THE ARCHIVED DDL AT `20260804130000_event_provider_foundation.sql:95-113` IS THE COLUMN CONTRACT AND IT IS COMPLETE. All 16 columns are transcribed and cross-checked against every column all three consumers select or write: the worker's status/run_after/priority/id/provider/job_type/payload/attempt_count/max_attempts/locked_at/locked_by/last_error_code/last_error_summary/updated_at, the admin surface's id/provider/job_type/status/attempt_count/run_after/last_error_code, and the connect route's provider/job_type/dedupe_key/payload/status/priority/updated_at. No gap and no guess, and NOTHING WAS INVENTED TO MAKE A QUERY RESOLVE. The status CHECK is complete for the reachable code, not merely convenient: the five values the worker writes are `running`, `queued`, `failed`, `dead`, `succeeded` and the two the routes read are `queued`, `running`, `dead` - five of the six admitted literals. The sixth, `cancelled`, is a soft-terminal state written by nothing today, and the set is transcribed IN FULL rather than narrowed to the five in use, because narrowing a soft-cancel out of a CHECK to make an audit read tidier is a real behavioural change.

THE PARTIAL DEDUPE INDEX IS TRANSCRIBED AND THE ROUTE'S `onConflict` IS ROUTED, NOT 'FIXED' SCHEMA-SIDE. This is the one place where the archive and a live consumer disagree, and it is the substantive finding of this task. `connect/route.ts:70` upserts with `{ onConflict: "dedupe_key" }`, which the Data API renders as a bare `ON CONFLICT (dedupe_key)`. PostgreSQL does not infer a PARTIAL unique index as an ON CONFLICT arbiter unless the statement supplies the index predicate as an arbiter `WHERE`, which PostgREST cannot emit, so the statement fails with SQLSTATE 42P10. Measured, and measured in BOTH directions so the fault is not misattributed: the arbiter-WHERE form of the same statement resolves; the archived index rejects a second ACTIVE job on a key (23505) and accepts the same key again once the job left `queued`/`running`. THE TEMPTING SCHEMA FIX IS THEREFORE WRONG, and measurement is why: a full unique index on `dedupe_key` is the only schema change that would make the route's bare arbiter resolve, and it would convert 'one ACTIVE job per dedupe key' into 'one job per dedupe key FOREVER' - so a connection could never be re-verified (the connect route keys `bandsintown:verify:${connection.id}`) and a `dead` job could never be re-enqueued. This lane does not make that change unilaterally. Two named options for the integrations lane, which owns the route: (a) ROUTE-SIDE, preferred and smallest - drop the `onConflict` and do a select-then-insert-or-update, which is the shape the ticketing lane already uses for the identical `idx_ticket_analytics_events_dedupe_key` partial index (`lib/ticketing/analytics.ts:66-80` handles 23505 rather than relying on inference), or add the predicate as an arbiter WHERE if a raw RPC is ever introduced; (b) SCHEMA-SIDE - a full unique index on `dedupe_key`, which is a semantic change requiring an explicit owner decision, and which this file records as NOT taken. Until one of them lands, `connect` is still 503 on the capability gate, so the defect is latent rather than an outage - but it is the next failure the moment `external_event_providers` is enabled, and it should not be discovered then.

NO QUEUE EXTENSION IS ADDED, AND THAT IS A NAMED DECISION FOR ANOTHER OWNER. The archive's own comment at `:94` calls this a 'durable queue ... claimed by cron workers', so a queue IS implied - but it names no extension, nothing in the active chain names one, and `pgmq` appears nowhere in this repository. The archived contract is a hand-rolled LEASE queue: `locked_at`/`locked_by` with a compare-and-set claim, `attempt_count`/`max_attempts` with bounded exponential backoff, and `dead` as a terminal state. This file transcribes it and adds no `create extension`. Whether Tourify should standardise on `pgmq` for provider sync work is an integrations/Release decision and is recorded here as such rather than settled by a transcription lane quietly pulling an extension into the chain. Recorded for the record: the lease claim at `cron/events/sync/route.ts:79-86` is a compare-and-set (`.eq('id', …).eq('status','queued')`), so two workers cannot both win one job - a property of live code, not of this schema, and one the index `idx_event_sync_jobs_claim` supports via the worker's exact sort order `(status, run_after, priority, id)`.

THE GRANT TO `authenticated` IS *NOTHING*, AND THAT IS THE ARCHIVE'S OWN POSITION RATHER THAN A NARROWING OF IT. This is the one deliberate difference from the sibling table, and it runs the other way. The archive grants nothing on `event_sync_jobs` to `anon` or `authenticated` (`:217`), states the reasoning at `:210-211` ('no client access. Service role bypasses RLS. No policies => deny all for anon/authenticated'), and DB-020 narrowed the sibling's `select, insert, update` grant to SELECT only. Here there is nothing to narrow: all three verified consumers resolve `.from()` through `createServiceRoleClient()`, so no `authenticated` grant is needed by any of them. AC-3 ANSWERED DIRECTLY: the connect route does not read this table at all - it service-role-WRITES it - and there is no unauthenticated read of it anywhere in the repository, so NO `authenticated` GRANT IS WARRANTED FOR ANY OF THE THREE ROUTES. `payload` is a provider-controlled JSON blob, so a speculative grant here would be unused client-reachable surface on a queue.

THE THREE REVISES ARE EXPLICIT RATHER THAN INHERITED, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING. A Supabase `postgres` role commonly carries `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT ALL ON TABLES TO postgres, anon, authenticated, service_role`, so a bare `create table` on a real target can hand a client-WRITABLE job queue to every signed-in user before a single explicit grant is issued. `revoke all on public.event_sync_jobs from public, anon, authenticated` is what makes the applied state independent of a default-privileges setting this chain does not manage in SQL (there is no `alter default privileges` anywhere in the active chain). House precedent: `20260823031000_integration_token_vault.sql:45` (VEN-016) does exactly this for its server-only vault, and three of the eight repair controls in the harness inject each of the three grants and prove the apply repairs them.

THE `to service_role` POLICY IS PURELY DEFENSIVE HERE, AND THAT IS A NARROWER CLAIM THAN THE SIBLING'S. DB-020 argued its service-role arm as a rescue for a route that is REACHABLE TODAY (`bandsintown/disconnect` has no capability gate at all). NO consumer of this table is reachable today, so the arm is justified differently and the difference is stated rather than copied: on Supabase, where `service_role` carries BYPASSRLS, `event_sync_jobs_service_role_all FOR ALL TO service_role` is a no-op; on a target where it does not, its absence would make all three routes fail closed with 42501. It grants `anon` and `authenticated` nothing, it is not a client policy, and it does not weaken RLS - with NO policy at all, RLS would DENY the role, so the policy strictly enables what RLS would otherwise block. It is measured in both configurations (BYPASSRLS on, and BYPASSRLS removed with the catalog change asserted). Because the role list IS the security contract for this relation - there are no client policies - the post-condition asserts the policy's ROLE LIST rather than only its existence, so a policy scoped to `authenticated` or to `PUBLIC` is reported by name. That is a stricter assertion than the sibling makes and it is the right one here.

NO DELETE PATH EXISTS FOR ANY NON-OWNER, AND THAT IS A CHOICE. No consumer deletes a job: `cron/events/sync` moves a job to `failed`/`dead`/`succeeded` and `cancelled` is the soft-terminal state, so the row and its error history are preserved. There is therefore no DELETE grant to `service_role` (which needs select, insert and update only - exactly the union of what the three consumers perform) and no client policy of any kind, and the post-condition asserts BOTH absences, so a future permissive delete cannot appear unnoticed. The ACL comparison is one key per (grantee, privilege) pair for exactly this reason: an extra DELETE is an extra key and so is reported UNEXPECTED, naming the defect rather than making the whole expected entry disappear.

THE `private`-SCHEMA STRANDED-RELATION CASE IS A REPAIR, NOT A REFUSAL, AND THAT IS THE FINDING AGAIN. The harness measures it rather than assuming it: `create table if not exists public.event_sync_jobs` finds nothing in `public`, creates a correct and EMPTY relation, the post-condition is satisfied, and any pre-existing rows stay stranded in the other schema. Measured: 2 rows left in `private`, 0 in the freshly created `public` relation. The guard repairs the public surface and silently orphans the data, so 'the relation exists in `public`' is a Layer 0 STOP CONDITION in the preflight rather than something this file can detect. Same class as `20260821025543:9`, where `search_path = private, public` put `ticketing_migration_issues` where no public reader could see it. This is now the second lane to measure it rather than predict it, and both measured the same way.

NO FUNCTION, TRIGGER, VIEW OR MATERIALIZED VIEW IS CREATED, so nothing is added to the routine inventory and the CP-016 regeneration delta is the single new relation plus three indexes. In particular the post-condition's expression normalization is a sequence of `regexp_replace` calls in one loop rather than a `create function` helper: a function declared inside a plpgsql `declare` block is not valid plpgsql (a function is not a declaration), and a top-level one would add a chain routine that no consumer wants and that the regeneration delta would then have to account for.

THE POST-CONDITION NORMALIZES RENDERED EXPRESSIONS, BECAUSE A TEXTUAL COMPARISON REPORTS A HEALTHY TARGET AS A VIOLATION. `pg_get_expr` renders `public.x` as `x` when `public` is in `search_path`, and renders an inlined SQL function as `( SELECT auth.uid() AS uid)` on a target whose `auth.uid()` is a SQL function and as `auth.uid()` on a real Supabase target whose is plpgsql - and this file controls neither. That is DB-013's recorded false-failure in a new form. Normalization is case, `public.` qualification, an inlined-function alias, whitespace, and redundant outer parentheses applied repeatedly. ITS LIMIT IS STATED: removing balanced parentheses is not injective, so the contract entries are written to be unambiguous under it, which for 16 column descriptors, one predicate, three index definitions, one policy and a grant matrix they are. The `polcmd` question is answered by the contract rather than by a branch - `using=` and `check=` are emitted for every policy and the expected list declares which is `-`.

NO TYPE REGENERATION IS NEEDED FOR THE FILE TO BE SAFE BUT IT IS NEEDED FOR THE DIAGNOSTICS TO CLEAR, AND IT IS BLOCKED. `lib/database.types.ts` is byte-unchanged (SHA-256 168daaff01fb7ef285fb7bc69cfb5876cb092491953cdbbb2cea3fa7cb7558ab7, verified against the value DB-020 recorded, and `git diff` shows no change to it or to `types/database.types.ts` / `types/supabase.ts`) and is NOT regenerated and NOT hand-edited. The file adds one relation, so the chain becomes one relation AHEAD of the contract: regeneration may only ADD coverage and delete nothing, which is the CP-016 superset property this file preserves. Regeneration remains blocked on RELEASE-013 provisioning a chain-built target, and `--linked` must never be used as a source (CP-127). Note the specific shape of the diagnostics here: because all three consumers use an untyped service-role client, they emit NO `tsc` diagnostic at all, so there are no diagnostics to clear for this table and no claim is made that this file clears any.

THE HARNESS LIVES INSIDE THIS MANIFEST'S DIRECTORY, NOT IN `supabase/tests/`, AND THAT IS A GRANT BOUNDARY RATHER THAN A CHOICE. `supabase/tests/**` is outside DB-021's working set, which names exactly this migration and `docs/engineering/migration-validation/**`; `package.json` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` are other lanes'. The consequence is real and is not hidden: `npm run check:db008-harness` does NOT run this harness, so nothing in CI executes this proof. It is reproducible by hand (`bash docs/engineering/migration-validation/db021_event_sync_jobs.harness.sh`) and by nobody's behalf until the wiring is granted. No CI coverage is claimed for it.
layeredPlan: Layer 0 (preflight, read-only, operator). Run the rowCountQueries and record the result. FOUR items are STOP CONDITIONS, not warnings. (a) `public.event_sync_jobs` must NOT already exist. It is expected absent on every environment; a non-NULL result means it exists out of band, and then `create table if not exists` will not touch it, this file will install forced RLS, a service-role policy and a grant on an unknown shape, and - if it is in a different schema - the stranded-row case measured in the harness applies: the public surface is repaired and the data is orphaned. (b) `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role` must all exist. The revokes, the grant and the `to service_role` policy are unguarded, so a target missing a role fails with 42704 - a loud, legible failure, which is why no guard wraps them. (c) `gen_random_uuid()` must be callable, which needs PostgreSQL 13+ built-in or `pgcrypto`; every Supabase target qualifies. There is no (d): this relation has NO foreign key, so no `auth.users` dependency exists - which the post-condition asserts as a positive claim (`constraint:fk:count=0`) rather than leaving unstated. Also record, without stopping on it: whether the target's `postgres` role carries default privileges granting anything to `anon`/`authenticated`/`PUBLIC` on new public tables (expected YES on a real Supabase project, which is exactly why this file's revokes are explicit), and whether `service_role` currently holds DELETE through a platform default-privilege grant, which this file does not issue and does not revoke - see the residual in `recovery`.

Layer 1 (apply, single run, operator). One transaction, this file only, manual and explicit. Never `supabase db reset`, never `db push --include-all`, never a forced or full-chain replay (CP-051). The order inside the file is: CREATE TABLE, three CREATE INDEX statements, COMMENT, ENABLE and FORCE RLS, one drop+create policy pair, one revoke and one grant, then the post-condition DO block. The post-condition is INSIDE the same transaction, so a target that cannot reach the asserted state fails the apply rather than reporting success. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change and in any order relative to every other migration: it creates one new relation, reads no existing row, writes no data row, and touches no existing object.

Layer 2 (postflight, read-only, operator). Run the postflight queries. The three that matter are the ANON probe, the AUTHENTICATED probe, and the SERVICE-ROLE probe, because unlike the sibling table there is NO own-row predicate to test here: the contract is that a client cannot read the table AT ALL, so an empty result would be a functional false-denial to investigate and a permission error is the correct outcome. `anon` SELECT must be a permission error, not an empty list. `authenticated` SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must ALL be permission errors - a single granted SELECT would be a client-readable provider-payload queue, and three of the eight repair controls exist to prove the apply removes exactly that. The service-role probe must return rows. Then run the two route-shaped statements verbatim, because they are the queries that return 500 today.

Layer 3 (no fourth layer in this lane). FOUR items are routed rather than absorbed: `event_sync_runs` (same archived file, still absent, and it alone keeps `cron/events/sync` and `admin/event-sync` broken - see the handoff), the `onConflict: "dedupe_key"` route defect and its two named fixes (integrations owns the route), the `pgmq`-versus-lease-table standardisation decision (integrations/Release), and CP-016 regeneration. None is required for this file to be safe, and none is claimed as done.

execution.resumeStrategy: Authored - manual apply pending (CP-051). One transaction, one file. The relation is created EMPTY by this migration, so there is no data lock: CREATE TABLE takes catalog locks only, all three CREATE INDEX statements build over zero rows, ENABLE/FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and the policy and grant statements take catalog locks, and the post-condition reads only catalog tables (`pg_class`, `pg_attribute`, `pg_attrdef`, `pg_constraint`, `pg_index`, `pg_policy`, `pg_roles`) and `aclexplode`. The lock budget is therefore independent of any existing data volume, which is a property of creating a table rather than of the statements. Safe to apply in any order relative to every other migration: this file touches no existing relation. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change. The file is re-runnable, so a re-apply is a no-op rather than an error.
execution.idempotency: Deterministic and repeatable, verified by applying the file FOUR times consecutively on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster, each in a single transaction (`psql -1`): the first three applies were consecutive and the FOURTH after 2 rows had been seeded. Every apply exited 0. `create table if not exists` skips on applies 2-4, the three `create [unique] index if not exists` guards skip or re-issue cleanly, the `drop policy if exists` + `create policy` pair re-issues cleanly, the revoke and grant are re-issued, and the post-condition passed after each. The seeded data survived the fourth apply: 2 rows before and 2 rows after, with `dedupe_key` and `payload->>'connectionId'` intact, exactly ONE `idx_event_sync_jobs_dedupe_active` and exactly THREE non-constraint indexes after four applies. The state after each of the first three was asserted at 16 columns / 1 policy / 3 indexes rather than inferred. This is the property the archived `20260804130000` file's own create would also have on an empty target, but it is measured here rather than assumed, and the fourth apply is the one that matters because it is the one that ran against a populated table.

quarantine.table: public.event_sync_jobs (created here; nothing is migrated into it and no existing table is read)
quarantine.strategy: No data movement, no backfill, no batch, no quarantine table. This file creates one empty relation and writes no row to it. There is no partial-application state to quarantine: the file is one transaction and its own post-condition RAISEs if the asserted state is unreachable, so a relation that ended up with the wrong column contract, the wrong policy, the wrong RLS setting or the wrong grants cannot be committed. The one state worth naming is the stranded-relation case measured in the harness: if a relation of this name already exists in ANOTHER schema, this file creates a correct and empty `public` one, leaves the other schema's rows where they are, and reports success. That is a Layer 0 stop condition, not a runtime branch, because detecting it and refusing would trade a loud, actionable operator message for a silent data orphan.
quarantine.lockBudget: No statement reads a row of any table. The post-condition is entirely catalog reads plus `aclexplode`, so it cannot queue behind a data lock, and the lock cost does not scale with the size of any catalogue. There is no statement here that holds a lock while waiting on another, so there is no deadlock ordering to get wrong.

constraints: THE STATUS CHECK IS THE ARCHIVED ONE AND IS ASSERTED BY ITS ADMITTED LITERAL SET RATHER THAN BY NAME OR BY TEXT, INCLUDING `cancelled`. `status in ('queued','running','succeeded','failed','dead','cancelled')` is the set the worker and the admin surface depend on. The post-condition extracts the literal set from the rendered expression, because PostgreSQL renders an IN-list with casts that differ between versions while the admitted values do not. The harness weakens the CHECK so `cancelled` is no longer storable and confirms the post-condition refuses, AND separately proves behaviourally that all six are storable and that a seventh (`paused`) is rejected - which is what makes the 'including cancelled' claim a measured one rather than a transcription assertion.

THE PRIMARY KEY IS ASSERTED AS A COLUMN SET (`{id}`) and the ABSENCE OF ANY FOREIGN KEY IS ASSERTED AS A POSITIVE CLAIM (`constraint:fk:count=0`) rather than left unstated. This matters more here than the sibling's FK: `create table if not exists` would leave a pre-existing relation's foreign keys in place, and an added FK is a dependency on a relation this file does not own. A `job -> connection` reference would be exactly the invention this lane refuses to make, and `event_sync_runs` (out of scope) is the relation that legitimately points at this one. The harness adds a foreign key to `auth.users` and confirms the post-condition refuses.

NO POLICY IS WEAKENED. There is no pre-existing policy on this relation on any environment, because the relation exists on no environment. The single policy's RENDERED PREDICATE, its `polcmd`, and - the part that is specific to this relation - its ROLE LIST are all asserted, so a policy scoped to `authenticated` or `PUBLIC` is reported by name. An EXTRA policy, a widened predicate, and a narrowed `polcmd` are all unexpected keys, so the same comparison reports each in either direction. Three controls cover policies: an `authenticated` SELECT, a `PUBLIC` SELECT, and an `authenticated` DELETE, plus a repair control that replaces the service-role policy with a `FOR SELECT` version and proves the apply restores `FOR ALL`.

NO GRANT IS WEAKENED AND NONE IS ASSUMED. `anon` and `authenticated` receive nothing, `PUBLIC` receives nothing, and `service_role` receives exactly insert/select/update. This is asserted as the RENDERED ACL, one key per (grantee, privilege) pair, with the owner's implicit privileges excluded by `grantee <> relowner`. That form is strictly stronger than a per-role `has_table_privilege` checklist and was chosen for a MEASURED reason rather than a stylistic one: the migration's first draft emitted one `acl:{ROLE}:{all privileges}` key, and the harness caught the consequence - granting `service_role` DELETE made the expected key disappear, so the defect was reported as 'MISSING', naming a REMOVAL for an ADDITION. Per-privilege keys report each in the correct direction. `service_role granted DELETE` is a refusal control; the three client-role and PUBLIC grants are REPAIR controls, because the file re-issues `revoke all ... from public, anon, authenticated` and so removes the drift before the post-condition is reached - which is the stronger claim and is what makes these the realistic defects on a Supabase target with default privileges.
indexes: THREE indexes are created, all transcribed from the archive at `:116-126`. `idx_event_sync_jobs_dedupe_active` is a UNIQUE index on `(dedupe_key) where status in ('queued','running') and dedupe_key is not null`; `idx_event_sync_jobs_claim` is on `(status, run_after, priority, id) where status = 'queued'`, which is exactly the worker's sort order; `idx_event_sync_jobs_stale_locks` is on `(locked_at) where status = 'running'`, so it can only ever answer the stale-lock question the worker asks. Every partial predicate is the point: an index for due work, for active dedupe, or for stale locks over rows that can never be in that state is an index that answers a question nobody asks.

Each index is asserted by its WHOLE rendered `pg_get_indexdef`, predicate included, and the harness proves three of them cannot be fooled: the dedupe index de-uniqued (the real cost of `create unique index if not exists`, which KEEPS a same-named non-unique index and silently removes the dedupe guarantee while reporting success), the claim index de-predicated, and the stale-lock index de-predicated. The claim index is additionally proved USABLE, not merely present, by running the worker's claim query under `set enable_seqscan = off` and asserting the plan names it - a planner choice on a 2-row fixture would be a vacuous control.

`idx_event_sync_jobs_dedupe_active` is a bare `create unique index`, NOT a UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, so it has no `pg_constraint` entry and IS compared. The primary key's backing index is excluded from the comparison: its column set is already asserted by the `constraint:p:{id}` entry and its backing index carries a PostgreSQL-generated name, which is a naming decision rather than a decision this file makes.

The predicate of the dedupe index is a SEMANTIC contract, not an optimisation, and it is measured behaviourally rather than left as a claim: a second ACTIVE job on a key is rejected with 23505; the same key is accepted again once the first job left `queued`/`running`; and `dedupe_key IS NULL` rows are uncollided (three stored). Those three together are why a full unique index on `dedupe_key` was NOT added to make the connect route's `onConflict` resolve - see the assumptions.
constraintsAndIndexes.validationPlan: The file's own post-condition DO block is the target-side validation, and it is proven able to FAIL in TWELVE ways, each measured by applying the file against a deliberately broken state on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15, each reported by name, and each with its fixture restored AND the migration re-applied and asserted green after the restore. The twelve refusals: an extra permissive `USING (true)` SELECT scoped to `authenticated`; the same scoped to `PUBLIC`; a client DELETE policy; `service_role` granted DELETE; the dedupe index de-uniqued; the claim index de-predicated; the stale-lock index de-predicated; `provider` retyped from `text` to `varchar`; `payload` made nullable; an extra column; an invented foreign key; the status CHECK narrowed so `cancelled` is no longer storable. FOUR of the twenty controls are REPAIRS rather than refusals, and the distinction is the finding rather than a naming preference: the file re-issues `alter table ... force row level security`, the top-level `drop policy` + `create policy` pair, `revoke all ... from public, anon, authenticated` and the `grant`, so drift in those is corrected by the apply and the post-condition is never reached with the defect present. Each repair control injects the drift, asserts the catalog really moved off the wanted value, applies, and asserts the value is restored. A FIFTH case - a relation stranded in `private`, the `20260821025543` precedent - is RECLASSIFIED from a refusal to a repair after measurement, because the file does not refuse it: it creates a correct empty `public` relation and orphans the rows, which is recorded in `assumptions` and as a Layer 0 stop condition. The post-condition reports BOTH failure directions in ONE message; its first draft raised on the ABSENT pass first, and the harness caught that a REPLACEMENT defect (a re-typed column, an added foreign key) could then only ever be reported as 'MISSING', with the 'what is actually there now' half unreachable. Behaviourally, as real identities on the same cluster: `anon` and `authenticated` are permission errors on select, insert, update and delete; the rendered ACL is exactly `service_role:insert,select,update`; and with `alter role service_role nobypassrls` applied, its exit code checked and the catalog re-read to confirm `rolbypassrls = f`, the admin SELECT, the worker's compare-and-set UPDATE with its RETURNING clause, and the connect route's upsert all still succeeded through the policy alone. 97 PASS / 0 FAIL, byte-identical across two runs.

recovery.rollback: There is no data to roll back, because the relation is created empty and this file writes no row to it. Rolling back means `DROP TABLE public.event_sync_jobs;` issued as a LATER FORWARD MIGRATION, never as an edit to this file, and it is only safe while the relation is still empty and no consumer has written to it. The operator should say plainly in the release ticket that rolling back returns `POST /api/integrations/bandsintown/connect`, `POST /api/cron/events/sync` and `GET /api/admin/event-sync` to a 500 on their own absent-relation path - which is the state every deployed environment is in today, so it is a truthful regression to a known-broken state and not a new one, though all three are capability-gated and therefore unreachable in practice. `ALTER TABLE ... NO FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and `REVOKE ... FROM anon, authenticated, PUBLIC` are NOT part of any rollback: both narrow the table's protection and the file's whole security argument is that RLS is the boundary here, with zero client policies as the only access control.
recovery.forwardFix: Any correction is a new additive migration with a higher version. Two shapes are already anticipated by this file's post-condition, so a bad forward fix cannot be applied silently: an extra policy, an extra privilege or an extra column is reported as UNEXPECTED, and a changed column contract, de-predicated index, missing grant or added foreign key is reported as MISSING - both name the defect and abort the apply, in the same message. Three forward fixes are anticipated by NAME rather than merely accommodated. (1) Adding `event_sync_runs` with its `job_id` FK to this relation: harmless here, because the post-condition asserts only what is ON this relation, and the FK lives on the other side. (2) Widening the grant to a client role: reported as UNEXPECTED, so the grant change and this file's expectations must move together - which is the intended behaviour, not an obstacle. (3) The `onConflict` fix: EITHER a route-side change, which touches no DDL at all, OR a full unique index on `dedupe_key`, which would be reported as UNEXPECTED here (`index:{idx_event_sync_jobs_dedupe_active}` would still be present but the new index would be an unclaimed key) and would require an explicit owner decision recorded before it is authored. A forward fix cannot silently widen the service-role policy's role list either: the role list is compared, not merely the policy's existence.

queries: SELECT count(*) AS columns, string_agg(attname, ',' ORDER BY attnum) AS column_list FROM pg_attribute WHERE attrelid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass AND attnum>0 AND NOT attisdropped; -- expect 16 and the archived list exactly

SELECT c.relrowsecurity AS rls_enabled, c.relforcerowsecurity AS rls_forced FROM pg_class c WHERE c.oid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass; -- expect true / true. FORCE is load-bearing here, not decorative: there are zero client policies, so this flag is the only thing holding an owner-privileged session back

SELECT polname, polcmd, polroles, pg_get_expr(polqual, polrelid) AS using_expr, pg_get_expr(polwithcheck, polrelid) AS check_expr FROM pg_policy WHERE polrelid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass ORDER BY polname; -- expect EXACTLY 1: event_sync_jobs_service_role_all, cmd=*, polroles={service_role}, using=true, check=true. A second row here is a client-reachable provider-payload queue and is the CP-104 shape

SELECT string_agg(coalesce(r.rolname,'PUBLIC')||':'||lower(a.privilege_type), ' ' ORDER BY coalesce(r.rolname,'PUBLIC'), a.privilege_type) AS acl_excluding_owner FROM pg_class c CROSS JOIN LATERAL aclexplode(c.relacl) a LEFT JOIN pg_roles r ON r.oid = a.grantee WHERE c.oid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass AND a.grantee <> c.relowner; -- expect exactly 'service_role:insert service_role:select service_role:update'. Any `anon:`, `authenticated:` or `PUBLIC:` entry is a client-reachable queue; any `service_role:delete` is an unreviewed delete path

SELECT has_table_privilege('anon','public.event_sync_jobs','select,insert,update,delete') AS anon_anything, has_table_privilege('authenticated','public.event_sync_jobs','select') AS authenticated_select, has_table_privilege('service_role','public.event_sync_jobs','select,insert,update') AS service_write, has_table_privilege('service_role','public.event_sync_jobs','delete') AS service_delete; -- expect false / false / true / false

-- THE ANON PROBE. Expect a PERMISSION ERROR, not an empty result. SELECT count(*) FROM public.event_sync_jobs; as `anon`. An empty result with no error would mean a grant exists that the file did not intend.

-- THE AUTHENTICATED PROBE, and it needs FOUR statements, not one. As a signed-in user: SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE against public.event_sync_jobs. ALL FOUR must be permission errors. Unlike the sibling table there is no own-row policy to scope, so the contract is that a client cannot touch this relation at all; a single granted SELECT publishes every job's payload, dedupe_key, locked_by and last_error_summary to every signed-in user.

-- THE SERVICE-ROLE PROBE. Expect rows, not an error. SELECT id, provider, job_type, status, attempt_count, run_after, last_error_code FROM public.event_sync_jobs WHERE status IN ('queued','running','dead') ORDER BY run_after LIMIT 100; as the service role, which is what admin/event-sync uses.

-- THE CONNECT ROUTE'S EXACT UPSERT, run as the service role. insert into public.event_sync_jobs (provider, job_type, dedupe_key, payload, status, priority, updated_at) values ('bandsintown','verify_connection','bandsintown:verify:<connection id>', '{"connectionId":"<connection id>"}'::jsonb, 'queued', 50, now()) on conflict (dedupe_key) do update set updated_at = excluded.updated_at returning id, status; -- EXPECT SQLSTATE 42P10, "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification". THIS IS THE MEASURED DEFECT, NOT AN APPLY FAILURE: idx_event_sync_jobs_dedupe_active is PARTIAL and PostgreSQL will not infer a partial unique index as an ON CONFLICT arbiter without the predicate as an arbiter WHERE, which the Data API cannot emit. A 42P10 here is the CORRECT applied state and confirms the harness finding; it is the route that is wrong, not the migration. See the assumptions for the two named fixes and the owner.

-- THE WORKER'S CLAIM, verbatim, as the service role. UPDATE public.event_sync_jobs SET status='queued', locked_at=NULL, locked_by=NULL WHERE status='running' AND locked_at < now() - interval '5 minutes'; then SELECT id FROM public.event_sync_jobs WHERE status='queued' AND run_after <= now() ORDER BY priority, id LIMIT 1; then the compare-and-set UPDATE ... SET status='running', locked_at=now(), locked_by='<worker>' WHERE id='<id>' AND status='queued' RETURNING id, provider, job_type, payload, attempt_count, max_attempts; -- the claim must affect exactly one row, and a second concurrent worker must get zero

SELECT pg_get_indexdef(i.indexrelid) FROM pg_index i JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=i.indexrelid WHERE i.indrelid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass AND c.relname IN ('idx_event_sync_jobs_dedupe_active','idx_event_sync_jobs_claim','idx_event_sync_jobs_stale_locks') ORDER BY c.relname; -- expect all three WITH their predicates; a FULL index here means a same-named index already existed out of band

SELECT conname, pg_get_expr(conbin, conrelid) AS predicate, convalidated FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass AND contype='c' ORDER BY conname; -- expect exactly one, on `status`, admitting all six literals including 'cancelled', and convalidated = true

SELECT count(*) AS foreign_keys FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='public.event_sync_jobs'::regclass AND contype='f'; -- expect 0. This relation has no foreign key in the archived contract; event_sync_runs is the relation that points at this one
